item.title: Heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause Dynamics Need Not Converge
item.description: arXiv:2610.20783v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a six-agent counterexample to convergence of scalar heterogeneous Hegselmann--Krause dynamics.
item.dc:creator: S. Rasoul Etesami, Behrouz Touri

item.title: Learning Warm Starts for the Simplex Method from Measured Solver Cost
item.description: arXiv:2610.20892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learned warm starts for the simplex method build starting bases using predictions of which variables will be basic at optimality. Prior work has shown that starting bases predicted by graph neural networks can sharply reduce iteration counts, but the time saved may fall well short of the iterations saved. On 25 classes of linear programs (LPs), we find that a strong supervised basis predictor removes two thirds of the dual simplex's iterations but only a third of its time. Two effects explain the gap: the iterations removed by a good start tend to be cheap, and closeness to an optimal basis does not rank starts by cost. We prove that two starts with equal overlap with an optimal basis and equal pivot counts can differ in linear-algebra work by a factor that grows with the square root of the number of rows. Empirically, across the starts of one LP, the pivot count explains 71% of the variance of log solve time, while the CPU instruction count explains 98.5%. We introduce CostStart, which uses supervised prediction for the basis and trains a small policy on measured instruction counts to choose, per LP, how many predicted columns to use, which algorithm and pricing rule to run, and whether to warm-start at all. On unseen LPs of the training classes, including LPs four times the training size, CostStart roughly halves the solve time relative to the solver's default start and is 1.4 to 2.2 times as fast as two published methods retrained on the same data.
item.dc:creator: Felix Parker, Danielle A. Ripsman, Emmett Springer, Kimia Ghobadi

item.title: Co-designing a Layered Control Architecture
item.description: arXiv:2610.20900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Layered control architectures (LCAs) are ubiquitous in complex engineering systems. However, in practice they are largely designed ad hoc and mostly dictated by the experience of the designer. This is because there is currently no systematic and practically applicable theory available to holistically design LCAs. Hence, systematically reasoning about the optimality, stability, and feasibility of the LCA design is not possible. We set a first step toward such a theory by presenting a framework for co-designing a two-layer LCA for a linear time-invariant plant. The resulting co-design problem optimizes over architectural design variables (e.g., reduced order model dimension and sampling ratio between the layers) and tuning-based design variables (e.g., the numerical values of the feedback gain or the matrices of the reduced order model), all subject to constraints that ensure stability, feasibility, and compute properties of the closed-loop LCA. The proposed formulation allows to make informed tradeoffs along the Pareto front traced over different axes of optimality, e.g., speed, accuracy or computational effort. We demonstrate the effect of making various tradeoffs in a simple numerical example.
item.dc:creator: Chris Verhoek, Charis Stamouli, George J. Pappas, Nikolai Matni

item.title: $\lambda$-geodesic convexity of the squared sliced-Wasserstein distance
item.description: arXiv:2610.20972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The squared Wasserstein distance with respect to a fixed target measure is not a convex function along Wasserstein geodesics over $\mathbb{R}^d$ when $d\geq 2$. Still, in dimension $d=1$, this function is $2$-geodesically convex. We prove that the square of the sliced-Wasserstein distance (which is a distance constructed averaging one-dimensional Wasserstein distances) is $\lambda$-geodesically convex (possibly with $\lambda \leq 0$) on sets of measures satisfying upper bounds on their density, when the target measure satisfies some given geometric conditions. We also present some consequences of this result in the study of the sliced-Wasserstein flow.
item.dc:creator: Giacomo Cozzi, Filippo Santambrogio

item.title: On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped Gradient Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.21026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In stochastic (strongly) convex optimization, establishing last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods has recently garnered increasing attention, as this not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these algorithms but also aligns more closely with practice. Notably, people have demonstrated that one of the most famous, simple, and popular methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent ($\mathtt{SGD}$), provably achieves last-iterate convergence. However, the existing results may have limited applicability, since they typically rely on strong conditions on the gradient noise (e.g., an exponentially decaying tail) rather than the more realistic heavy-tailed noise. Unfortunately, when faced with heavy-tailed noise, $\mathtt{SGD}$ is known to exhibit undesirable behavior or even fail to converge. To address the challenge of heavy-tailed noise, people have proposed $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$, an algorithm that combines $\mathtt{SGD}$ with a simple mechanism, gradient clipping. Although $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ performs well in practice, its last-iterate convergence property remains highly underexplored. In this work, we prove the first optimal last-iterate rates in high probability for $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ under heavy-tailed noise, thereby closing a gap in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Zijian Liu

item.title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles
item.description: arXiv:2610.21139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Swati Gupta, Tianjiao Li

item.title: Dual Representations and Proxy Characterization of $H_2$ Norm for Partial Integral Equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.21355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Duality and dual representations are essential tools for systems theory and controller synthesis. For any finite-dimensional causal linear time-invariant (CLTI) system, there exists a dual CLTI system with identical $H_\infty$ and $H_2$ norm. These relations are found by simply taking the adjoint of the transfer function. For nonlinear, time-varying or infinite-dimensional systems, however, such a transfer function may not exist or be difficult to obtain. For duality in the $H_\infty$ norm, this obstacle is overcome by using the equivalent time-domain, induced $L_2$-norm characterization. For $H_2$ norms there is no such equivalent characterization and hence proxy norms such as induced energy to peak and impulse to energy norms are used. These proxy norms bound the $H_2$ norm in the CLTI case. However, neither of these $H_2$ proxy norms equal the same $H_2$ proxy of the canonical dual representation. In this paper, we overcome this by proposing a dual representation whose induced energy to peak proxy equals the impulse to energy proxy of the primal and vice-versa. This relation is developed in the context of Partial Integral Equation (PIE) representations. The result is then used to establish primal-dual operator inequalities for both proxy norms similar in form to the primal-dual LMIs used to characterize the $H_2$ norm.
item.dc:creator: Danilo Braghini, Tristan Thomas, Sachin Shivakumar, Javad M. Velni, Matthew M. Peet

item.title: Observability as a constraint qualification for a nonsmooth bilevel PDE-constrained problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.21377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by experiment design for parameter identification in image reconstruction, we analyze a bilevel control problem involving sparse inversion at the lower level. Qualified optimality conditions in explicit multiplier form are shown to hold under either an observability condition for a coupled system or the Lebesgue nullity of a contact set induced by the lower-level adjoint variable. We prove that these conditions are independent of one another and that they cannot, in general, both be omitted. The approach is based on the characterization of local first-order geometric objects (tangent and normal cones) associated with a set of lifted constraints. Based on the resulting optimality conditions, we formulate a reduced gradient method and illustrate it through numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Christian Clason, Alberto Dom\'inguez Corella, Jyrki Jauhiainen

item.title: Optimization of a Perturbed Implicit Sweeping Process by Constrained Discontinuous Controls
item.description: arXiv:2610.21384v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies optimal control problems governed by an implicit sweeping process with velocity-dependent constraint geometry, where the dynamics are described by a differential inclusion involving the normal cone to a moving convex polyhedral set. Such systems form a challenging class of nonsmooth differential inclusions due to the implicit coupling between the state, velocity, and constraint reaction. To address these difficulties, we use a method of discrete approximations together with tools of variational analysis and generalized differentiation. This approach allows us to derive necessary optimality conditions for local minimizer in discrete-time problems and subsequently pass to the limit to obtain optimality conditions for the original continuous-time system. The obtained results extend existing optimal control theory for sweeping processes to a class of implicit dynamical systems with state-and velocity-dependent constraints.
item.dc:creator: Yen Dang, Boris S. Mordukhovich, Dao Nguyen

item.title: Kernel-Based Heterogeneous Mean Field Games on a Continuum Type Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.21423v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a class of heterogeneous mean field games on a continuum type space, in which interactions are generated by a Hilbert-Schmidt kernel operator acting on the type-indexed mean state profile. The control set is allowed to be a general closed convex subset of a Euclidean space, and the optimal feedback is characterized through the unique maximizer of the Hamiltonian. For a prescribed mean-field path, the stochastic maximum principle leads to a family of fully coupled forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) indexed by the agent type. Under Lipschitz conditions and a monotonicity assumption on the reduced coefficients, the frozen FBSDE is globally well posed. We then formulate the consistency problem as a fixed-point problem for the kernel mean-field path. When the operator norm of the interaction kernel is sufficiently small, the resulting map has an invariant ball and is continuous and compact, so that Schauder's theorem yields existence of a mean field Nash equilibrium. Uniqueness follows under an aggregate monotonicity condition adapted to the kernel coupling. A linear-quadratic example illustrates how finite-rank interactions and heterogeneous risk preferences produce coupled collective modes, and yields a spectral smallness condition for existence and an explicit sufficient condition for uniqueness.
item.dc:creator: Guangchen Wang, Luebo Xia

item.title: Restarted Fixed-Point Acceleration of Proximal ADMM for Capped-$\ell_1$ Penalized Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.21444v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider box-constrained optimization with a convex, Lipschitz continuous loss function that may be nonsmooth and a capped-$\ell_1$ penalty. Exploiting the convex branch representation of the capped-$\ell_1$ penalty, we construct an associated nonexpansive fixed-point mapping for each branch and, based on these mappings, propose a restarted accelerated proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (RA-pADMM). The resulting algorithm consists of a preliminary branch identification phase and a subsequent accelerated phase based on either the Halpern or fast Krasnosel'ski\u{i}--Mann iteration, together with a sufficient decrease restart mechanism. We prove that the preliminary phase terminates after finitely many iterations and that only finitely many branch updates are accepted during the subsequent phase. The primal iterates and proximal outputs converge to a common lifted stationary point, which is also a $\nu$-strong local minimizer of the corresponding cardinality penalized problem. Moreover, the Halpern and fast Krasnosel'ski\u{i}--Mann variants achieve nonergodic $O(k^{-1})$ and asymptotic $o(k^{-1})$ convergence rates, respectively, for both the objective value gap and the Karush--Kuhn--Tucker residual associated with the final branch. Numerical experiments on sparse recovery and real data classification problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RA-pADMM algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Hongyuan Tao, Fan Wu, Wei Bian

item.title: An Alternating Minimization Algorithm for Federated Sparse Orthogonal Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
item.description: arXiv:2610.21455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop an alternating minimization algorithm for federated sparse orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization (ONMF) with emphases on controlling client drift. To reduce communication frequency, clients perform multiple local updates between communication rounds, biasing updates toward their respective local objectives and giving rise to client drift, particularly under data heterogeneity. In federated sparse ONMF, global nonsmooth regularization further complicates drift control, as proximal mappings generally do not commute with averaging. To address these challenges, we develop an effective optimization algorithm that introduces variable splitting to decouple proximal operator evaluation from communication, allowing clients to handle joint sparsity regularization locally. In addition, the algorithm incorporates a correction term into the local gradients to adjust the update directions and mitigate client drift. We theoretically establish that the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear convergence to a bounded residual error under some mild conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate favorable convergence behavior on a synthetic dataset and competitive clustering performance on real-world multi-view datasets.
item.dc:creator: Yanjiao Zhu, Xianchao Xiu, Yongyang Xiong, Wanquan Liu

item.title: Descending Everest with First-Order Oracles: Oracle Complexity of Convex Optimization under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2610.21461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions, the curvature may grow together with the gradient norm. Therefore, even when $\|x^0-x^*\|\le R$, the gradient and the optimality gap at the starting point may be exponentially large in $L_1R$, and the bound $\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}$, known for the accelerated method on functions with Lipschitz gradient, no longer describes the complexity of the problem. We determine the oracle complexity of this class for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods: for $L_0R^2/\varepsilon\ge1$, the optimal number of oracle calls $N$ satisfies $1+N=\widetilde\Theta(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+L_1R)$. The upper bound reads $O(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(1+L_1R)\log(2+L_1R))$: the method first passes through the large-gradient regime in $O(1+L_1R)$ iterations with an inexact line search, and then the standard accelerated method with a constant stepsize takes over. The lower bound is obtained by means of chains and the orthogonal invariance principle on functions conjugate to strongly convex functions on a polytope. If the initial optimality gap is at most $4\varepsilon$, the optimal bound becomes $1+N=\widetilde\Theta(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(L_1R)^{2/3})$.
item.dc:creator: Mikhail Rudomanov, Ivan Fomin, Alexander V. Gasnikov, Fedor S. Stonyakin

item.title: Optimal First-Order Methods for a Class of Structured H\"older-Smooth Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convex optimization with H\"older-continuous gradients has attracted considerable attention as a framework bridging smooth and nonsmooth optimization. For this class, Nesterov's universal fast gradient method attains the optimal black-box complexity, and we study whether exploiting further problem structure can further improve this bound. In this paper, we study an important class of H\"older-smooth problems, namely regularized $\ell_p$ regression with $p\in(1,2)$, whose loss has a $(p-1)$-H\"older-continuous gradient and for which the universal method requires $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2/(3p-2)})$ iterations. Exploiting the problem structure, we characterize a family of smooth approximations based on $p$-Huber smoothing and prove that, for any prescribed smoothness level, it minimizes the worst-case approximation error among smooth lower approximations of the scalar loss. Combined with accelerated proximal gradients, the smoothing approach attains an $\varepsilon$-optimal solution in $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1/p})$ matrix--vector products, which significantly improves the complexity guarantee for $1<p<2$. We show that this bound is optimal by providing a matching lower bound. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate the practical performance of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Baiying Xin, Qi Deng

item.title: Data-driven Smooth-to-hard Spectral Regularization for General Linear Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The logistic smooth-to-hard shrinker is the proximal map of an explicit saturating spectral penalty for general linear inverse problems. Its exact weak convexity yields a unique scaled update and proximal-gradient stationarity guarantees, while independent validation provides finite-grid parameter-selection control. We use MRI as an illustrative example.
item.dc:creator: Guanzhong Yang, Zi Wang, Guang Yang

item.title: An Adaptive Cubic Regularisation Algorithm Based on Interior-Point Methods for Optimization with General Inequality Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2610.21673v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear constrained optimization has a wide range of practical applications. The interior-point method is considered to be one of the most powerful algorithms for solving nonlinear inequality constrained optimization. In this paper, we consider optimization with general inequality constraints and propose an Adaptive Regularisation algorithm using Cubics Based on Interior-Point methods (ARCBIP). For solving the barrier problem, we construct ARC subproblem with linearized constraints and the well-known fraction to the boundary rule that prevents slack variables from approaching their lower bounds prematurely. We employ a composite-step approach and reduced Hessian methods to deal with linearized constraints, where the trial step is decomposed into a normal step and a tangential step. They are obtained by solving two ARC subproblems approximately with the fraction to the boundary rule. Requirements on normal steps and tangential steps are given to ensure global convergence. To determine whether the trial step is accepted, we use exact penalty function as the merit function in ARC framework. The updating of the barrier parameter is implemented by adaptive strategies. Global convergence is analyzed under mild assumptions. Preliminary numerical experiments and some comparison results are reported.
item.dc:creator: Yonggang Pei, Jingyi Guo, Shuowen Fu, Zhuohan Li

item.title: On the Complexity of Finding Stationary Points in Stochastic $(L_0, L_1)$-Smooth Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.21692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity of finding $\epsilon$-stationary points of $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth nonconvex functions. Under bounded-variance noise, existing analyses of normalized and clipped stochastic gradient descent (SGD) establish optimal dependence on $\epsilon$ and $L_0$, but the jointly optimal dependence on $L_0$, $L_1$, and $\epsilon$ remains unclear. We resolve this question for an unbiased SFO whose gradient noise has a $p$th central moment bounded by $\sigma^p$ for some $\sigma\geq 0$, where $p\in(1,2]$.Specifically, we establish an SFO lower bound of $\Omega\big(\big(\sigma^{\frac{p}{p-1}}\epsilon^{-\frac{p}{p-1}}+1\big) (L_0 \Delta\epsilon^{-2}+L_1\Delta\epsilon^{-1})\big)$, where $\Delta>0$ is the initial optimality gap.This bound identifies an unavoidable contribution proportional to $L_1\epsilon^{-1}\Delta$. We also prove that mini-batch (smoothed) normalized SGD can attain a matching upper bound, thereby establishing the optimal SFO complexity.
item.dc:creator: Yanpeng Liang, Luo Luo

item.title: Strong NP-Hardness of Rank-2 Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
item.description: arXiv:2610.21874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) approximates a nonnegative matrix by the product of two nonnegative matrices with a prescribed inner dimension~$r$. The existence of an exact NMF can be decided in polynomial time for every fixed~$r$, and a best rank-$1$ NMF in the Frobenius norm can be obtained from a truncated singular value decomposition. We prove that computing a best rank-$2$ NMF in the Frobenius norm is strongly NP-hard. Our proof uses a polynomial-time reduction from \textsc{Clique} that produces symmetric positive-definite, completely positive matrices with polynomially bounded integer entries. The same reduction also establishes strong NP-hardness of rank-$2$ symmetric NMF.
item.dc:creator: Arnaud Vandaele

item.title: GPU Parallel Pareto Local Search for Multi-objective QUBO
item.description: arXiv:2610.21890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit Pareto Local Search (PLS) for multi-objective quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems. Multi-objective QUBO formulations have gained increasing attention as a universal modeling method and natural input for quantum optimization. While exact methods exist, their unconstrained binary structure makes them well-suited for heuristics such as PLS. At the same time, GPUs offer a powerful classical alternative to quantum-inspired optimization. We develop an efficient GPU-based parallel implementation of PLS for multi-objective QUBO problems. Our approach combines coarse-grained and fine-grained parallelization. On the coarse-grained level, an initial set of supported solutions is generated using weighted-sum optimization, from which multiple PLS processes are started in parallel. At the fine-grained level, neighborhood exploration is parallelized on the GPU by simultaneously evaluating binary-flip candidate solutions across all objectives. Non-dominated solutions are maintained using an ND-Tree data structure to support efficient Pareto updates. The implementation combines several known PLS techniques within a unified CPU/GPU hybrid architecture. We describe the algorithmic components, the GPU-specific design decisions, and report results from a computational study evaluating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Riedm\"uller, Thorsten Koch

item.title: Defense Filters for Robust Learning of Partially Observed Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.21935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robust estimation of unknown system dynamics from partial observations under attack is a core challenge in learning for control, increasingly critical in multi-agent networks subject to adversarial data poisoning. Existing methods either require highly restrictive assumptions on the adversary or yield weak error bounds. In this paper, we consider identifying partially observed linear dynamical systems subject to adversarial attacks with an attack probability $p < 0.5$ at each time. We propose a defense-filtering framework in which a system designer leverages knowledge of the observation matrix to construct a defense filter satisfying full column rank and subspace separability conditions, which enables the evaluation of a single-attack scenario against observed data. Using this framework, we analyze the constrained $\ell_2$-norm estimator and establish finite-sample error bounds for recovering the Markov parameter matrix $G^*$. This is the first approach to provide provable system identification guarantees via a defense filter for partially observed systems subject to harsh attack environments where the attack probability approaches $0.5$.
item.dc:creator: Jihun Kim, Javad Lavaei

item.title: Convergence Rates for Lasserre's Upper-Bound Hierarchy on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with Gaussian Measure
item.description: arXiv:2610.22030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish quantitative convergence rates for Lasserre's measure-based upper-bound hierarchy on $\mathbb{R}^d$ using the standard Gaussian measure as the reference measure. For any polynomial $f$ attaining its global infimum $f_{\min}$, we prove that the order-$r$ upper bounds satisfy $$ \lambda_r-f_{\min}=O\Big(\frac{1}{r}\Big), $$ yielding, to the best of our knowledge, the first explicit convergence rate for this hierarchy on a noncompact domain. We further show that the rate is sharp by proving an $\Omega(1/r)$ rate for $f=x^2$, while demonstrating that, without attainment of the infimum, convergence can be arbitrarily slow: for every $m\ge0$, we construct a polynomial whose upper bounds converge at rate $\Theta(r^{-1/(m+2)})$.
item.dc:creator: Sander Gribling, Igor Klep, Poornendu Kumar

item.title: Polarizable quasiconvex function generated metric projection
item.description: arXiv:2610.22106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study when generalized metric projections generated by strongly quasiconvex functions are polarizable. The point of departure is Moreau's decomposition theorem, where the Euclidean metric projections onto two mutually polar closed convex cones form complementary retractions whose sum is the identity. This suggests the following fundamental question: when does a given retraction admit such a complementary polar retraction? We formulate this notion through polarizable retractions and then specialize it to generalized projections of the form $x\mapsto P_{\cal C}^\varphi(x)$, defined by minimizing $\varphi(x-y)$ with respect to $y$ over a closed convex set ${\cal C}$. After recalling basic properties of mutually polar retractions and first-order characterizations of generalized projections, we prove the main result: If $\varphi$ is strongly quasiconvex, the generalized projection $P_{\cal C}^\varphi$ is polarizable if and only if ${\cal C}$ is a closed convex cone. Thus, polarizability of the projection is characterized by the conic geometry of its range.
item.dc:creator: A. B. N\'emeth, S. Z. N\'emeth

item.title: Event-Triggered Funnel Control for Output Reference Tracking of Unknown Nonlinear Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an event-triggered zero-order hold implementation of the funnel controller for output reference tracking of unknown nonlinear systems. The control input is updated only when the deviation between the current and the last transmitted input exceeds a prescribed threshold, reducing the number of input updates while maintaining closed-loop performance guarantees by incorporating an auxiliary integral state to compensate for the error introduced by the zero-order-hold input. We establish a uniform lower bound on the inter-event intervals excluding Zeno behavior, and show that the same closed-loop guarantees hold for any predefined sampling schedule with sufficiently short sampling intervals. The theoretical results are illustrated by numerical simulations.
item.dc:creator: Janina Schaa, Thomas Berger

item.title: Gradient-Hessian Query Tradeoffs: Matching Lower Bounds in Logarithmic Dimension
item.description: arXiv:2610.22208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish matching lower bounds for the tradeoff between gradient and Hessian queries in nonconvex optimization with Lipschitz Hessian. In normalized units, the initial objective gap is at most $T$, the Hessian Lipschitz constant is at most one, and the target gradient norm is one. For sufficiently large $T$, dimension $d \ge C\log(2+T)$, and a prescribed Hessian budget $h \ge 1$ with $h+1 \le aT$, every randomized algorithm requires $\Omega(\min\{Td^{1/3}, T^{3/2}/\sqrt{h+1}\})$ ordinary queries. An ordinary query returns the value and gradient; a Hessian query returns the complete second jet and is charged only to its own budget. Both budgets are worst-case caps. Queries and outputs may be arbitrary real points, and no Hessian-norm bound is imposed. The hard input law consists of fixed, globally $C^3$, coercive functions. The construction combines sequential readouts of a continuous random matrix with localized completion blocks and reliability dimensions that vary across hierarchy levels. Premature disclosures are charged by their expected task cost, while every oracle reply remains the exact jet of the presampled objective. This yields a logarithmic dimension threshold and a depth-independent third-derivative bound. Together with a translation of the NALEN upper bound of Chen, Liu, Luo, and Zhang, the result determines the query tradeoff up to absolute constants throughout the stated range.
item.dc:creator: Wendao Wu, Haihan Zhang, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin

item.title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.20925v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
item.dc:creator: Anutam Srinivasan, Siddhant Panse, Glen Chou

item.title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.21020v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study whether the classical momentum-based acceleration that improves the condition-number dependence of gradient descent from $\kappa$ to $\sqrt{\kappa}$ for strongly convex, smooth objectives extends to Gaussian variational inference (GVI) for strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. With exact Gaussian expectations, a convex composite formulation of GVI yields the classical accelerated $\sqrt{\kappa}$ convergence rate. However, when only pointwise derivatives are available, we construct a family of strongly log-concave targets for which any randomized algorithm requires $\kappa^{1-o(1)}$ queries to achieve a fixed objective accuracy, even when the initial objective gap is bounded independently of $\kappa$. Thus curvature bounds alone cannot guarantee uniform accelerated total-query complexity. We then ask which additional structure permits acceleration and give positive examples: under a Hessian-Lipschitz assumption, variance-reduced stochastic methods yield accelerated guarantees when the Hessian variation is sufficiently small. Finally, experiments on real datasets show substantial empirical speedups from acceleration across a broad range of methods.
item.dc:creator: Jaesung R. Park, Uijeong Jang, Yifan Chen

item.title: Matrix Completion Discriminants
item.description: arXiv:2610.21341v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce the matrix completion discriminant of a graph as the Zariski closure of the set of partial symmetric matrices whose completion fibers fail to meet a rank stratum transversely. A clique-sum formula for the matrix completion discriminant is established for arbitrary graphs, while explicit defining equations for cycles are obtained in terms of iterated resultants. Using these results together with the analysis of $K_4$-minor-free graphs, we prove that for every cycle-completable graph, the discriminant factors into determinant factors from maximal cliques and resultant factors from chordless cycles.
item.dc:creator: Yoshiyuki Sekiguchi, Shin-ichi Tanigawa

item.title: Honesty is the Best Policy ... or is it? Demand Management for Probabilistic Service Options
item.description: arXiv:2610.21351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: To enable well-informed customer choices and redistribute demand across service options, providers can display probabilities regarding predicted service levels at the time of booking, effectively offering probabilistic service options. In many service settings, the underlying truthful probabilities endogenously depend on the system state, rather than being static product attributes controlled by the provider. While customers rely on this information when making decisions, they cannot readily verify its accuracy. Consequently, providers may be tempted to manipulate the displayed probabilities to guide customers' choices in their favor, creating a novel lever for demand management. In this work, we model the resulting problem as a sequential decision process, define truthful probabilities recursively, and introduce transparency constraints that limit their distortion. Because the exact computation of truthful probabilities is intractable for realistic settings, we develop an adapted reinforcement learning algorithm to approximate them. Furthermore, we propose a sampling-based mixed-integer program to optimize the information communicated by the provider in each state. Our framework enables providers to gauge the benefits of dynamically disclosing probabilistic information at the time of booking and sheds light on incentives for manipulation. Our computational study is motivated by out-of-home delivery, i.e., the delivery to parcel lockers or shops, and reveals a trade-off between individual-level transparency and aggregate customer utilities.
item.dc:creator: Daniela Sailer, Robert Klein, Claudius Steinhardt

item.title: It Takes Two Moments: Rigidity and Limits of Continuous Encoders for Over-the-Air Computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.21536v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study over-the-air computation of functions, such as empirical variance, formed by combining two separately postprocessed sums of locally transformed observations. We consider continuous encoders subject to pointwise peak-power constraints over a single use of a complex multiple-access channel. With four or more transmitters, we identify conditions under which exact noiseless recovery forces every continuous encoder collection into a common affine structure that preserves both sums, reducing infinite-dimensional encoder design to selecting a finite set of coefficients. To quantify resilience against channel noise, we introduce a robustness score that measures the separation of noiseless received aggregates relative to variations in the desired function value. Within this characterized encoder family, we formulate robustness maximization as an exact convex semi-infinite program, eliminating rank constraints without a relaxation gap, and construct a decoder that attains the minimum uniform noise-amplification constant. For several function classes, including empirical variance, we derive closed-form robustness-optimal encoders and scores. Under mild regularity conditions, we also establish sharp limits on the Gaussian mean squared error at high signal-to-noise ratios and show how using the input distribution reduces average error at the expense of uniform robustness.
item.dc:creator: Saeed Razavikia

item.title: Quantum-compatible Riemannian conjugate gradient for ground-state preparation
item.description: arXiv:2610.21782v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Riemannian optimization provides a natural geometric framework for designing quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation, most notably through quantum imaginary-time evolution. However, existing geometry-aware approaches primarily employ steepest-descent updates, leaving more advanced methods from classical Riemannian optimization largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce quantum conjugate gradient descent (QCGD), a quantum-compatible implementation of Riemannian conjugate gradient that combines the steepest descent direction with information retained from previous search directions. In our numerical experiments, the proposed approach achieves faster convergence per iteration than the baseline double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE) algorithm, and we quantify the associated circuit cost with gate counts produced by Qrisp. This improvement, however, comes at the cost of increased circuit depth for each update step, revealing a trade-off between convergence rate and implementation complexity. Nevertheless, since the circuit depth for those algorithms grows exponentially with the number of iterations, the proposed method may offer practical advantages, particularly in the early fault-tolerant regime.
item.dc:creator: Andres Arcia-Lopez, Marek Gluza, Yudai Suzuki, Cyrus Mostajeran

item.title: Provably Efficient Risk-Sensitive Offline Reinforcement Learning via Optimized Certainty Equivalents
item.description: arXiv:2610.21870v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) addresses decision-making under uncertainty and adverse outcomes. Learning risk-sensitive policies from fixed datasets is important when additional interaction with the environment is costly. Existing work on risk-sensitive RL focuses on online settings or specific risk measures, leaving a general theoretical understanding of its offline setting underdeveloped. In this work, we investigate efficient offline risk-sensitive RL using the optimized certainty equivalent (OCE), a general class of risk measures. We consider two formulations: dynamic-OCE RL, which applies OCE recursively at each step, and static-OCE RL, which applies a single OCE to the cumulative rewards. Under the tabular setting, we develop pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for both formulations and establish tight sublinear suboptimality bounds, explicitly capturing how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty. Moreover, we establish minimax suboptimality lower bounds to characterize the problem's fundamental limits. To handle large state spaces, we further develop pessimistic least-squares value-iteration algorithms that incorporate the general OCE risk criterion into linear function approximation. We establish utility-dependent sublinear guarantees with explicit dependence on the feature dimension $d$. To our knowledge, we provide the first offline algorithms along with the first upper and lower suboptimality bounds for both dynamic- and static-OCE RL.
item.dc:creator: Hanzhen Wang, Boxiang Lyu, Zhongxiang Dai, Siyang Gao, Dake Zhang, Shuang Qiu

item.title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
item.description: arXiv:2610.21908v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Pedramfar, Siamak Ravanbakhsh

item.title: Per-State Signatures and Mean Time-to-Failure: An Algorithm for Systems With Simultaneous Failures
item.description: arXiv:2610.22181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present an algorithm that computes the structural signature and the mean time-to-failure (MTTF) of a monotone binary system at every one of its states, rather than only at the state in which all components work. It makes no assumption on the structure function and evaluates it exactly once per state, as many times as needed for the signature of the complete system alone, so computing the MTTF everywhere costs only a factor polynomial in the number of components over computing it once. As a by-product, it identifies all minimal path sets. We assume exchangeable component failure times whose survivor count is a continuous-time Markov chain. This setting admits simultaneous failures, as in the L\'evy-frailty Marshall-Olkin, binomial failure rate and lethal-shock models, where the simplifications available for single failures do not apply. We use the per-state MTTF to define threshold repair policies. We show that the per-state signature is a strictly finer decision criterion than the MTTF: signature dominance at a common failure count implies MTTF dominance, but not conversely. Under the L\'evy-frailty Marshall-Olkin model the MTTF is monotone in the state, which yields the long-run cost rate of every threshold policy in a single pass. Experiments on 22 benchmark networks with up to 30 components and 31 failure models show that the best MTTF-threshold policy has a median excess cost of 0.36% over the optimal state-based policy, and that it is never worse than the best policy that repairs after a fixed number of failures.
item.dc:creator: Guido Lagos, Sim\'on \'Avila

item.title: Near-Optimal Parallel $M$-Matrix Scaling
item.description: arXiv:2610.22302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of computing a positive diagonal scaling of a $d \times d$ symmetric $M$-matrix so that all row and column sums are $1$. We provide a poly-logarithmic iteration algorithm that solves this problem to high accuracy, where the cost of each iteration is dominated by the cost of solving a Laplacian system. This improves upon the recent $\tilde{O}(d^{1/3})$ iteration bound of [Vladu STOC 2025] and yields a randomized algorithm for the problem that runs in near-linear time and poly-logarithmic parallel depth.
item.dc:creator: Chih-Hung Liu, Aaron Sidford, Ta-Wei Tu

item.title: Stochastic internal habit formation and optimality
item.description: arXiv:2502.05081v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Growth models with internal habit formation have been studied in various settings under the assumption of deterministic dynamics. The purpose of this paper is to explore a stochastic version of the model in Carroll et al. [1997, 2000], one the most influential on the subject. The goal is twofold: on one hand, to determine how far we can advance in the technical study of the model; on the other, to assess whether at least some of the deterministic outcomes remain valid in the stochastic setting. The resulting optimal control problem proves to be challenging, primarily due to the lack of concavity in the objective function. This feature is present in the model even in the deterministic case (see, e.g., Bambi and Gozzi [2020]). We develop an approach based on Dynamic Programming to establish several useful results, including the regularity of the solution to the corresponding HJB equation and a verification theorem. There results lay the groundwork for studying the model optimal paths and comparing them with the deterministic case.
item.dc:creator: Michele Aleandri, Alessandro Bondi, Fausto Gozzi

item.title: Optimal Transport on Lie Group Orbits
item.description: arXiv:2508.09377v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In its most general form, the optimal problem is an infinite-dimensional optimization problem, yet certain notable instances admit closed-form solutions. We identify the common source of this tractability as \textit{symmetry} and formalize it using Lie group theory. Fixing a Lie group action and a reference distribution, we study optimal transport between measures in the same orbit. For such pairs of measures, restricting the Monge problem to transport maps induced by the group action yields the Lie group orbit transport problem, an optimization over the stabilizer of the reference law that provides an upper bound on the Monge problem. Under suitable regularity conditions, a feasible group-induced map satisfying a $c$-convex first-order certificate attains this bound, solves the original Monge problem, and induces an optimal Kantorovich plan. For the quadratic cost, we establish a structural criterion based on a global Cartan decomposition. Exploiting the nonuniqueness of orbit representations, the criterion constructs an optimal map through a path of group transformations with self-adjoint derivatives. Once verified for an action and reference law, it applies to every pair of orbit measures with finite second moments. For affine-induced actions, Cartan structure on the linear image suffices, and the means and covariance operators determine the optimal map and value explicitly. The framework recovers classical elliptical transport formulas and yields closed-form solutions on congruence orbits generated by absolutely continuous, spectrally invariant reference laws, including Wishart, inverse-Wishart, and matrix beta type~II families with fixed shape parameters. It also recovers the common-copula optimal coupling for multivariate normal sinh-arcsinh laws with unit tailweight parameters sharing a Gaussian copula, and evaluates the optimal transport value in closed form.
item.dc:creator: Bahar Taskesen

item.title: Robust Parallel Machine Scheduling: A Comparison of Robustness Measures and Local Search Approaches
item.description: arXiv:2512.15471v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many real-world scheduling problems, the processing times of tasks are subject to uncertainty. This makes it essential to design schedules that are robust against disruptions. We distinguish between two types of robustness: quality-robust schedules keep a stable objective value under disruptions, while solution-robust schedules keep a stable schedule structure. We study how to generate schedules for the Stochastic Parallel Machine Scheduling Problem (SPMSP) with precedence constraints and release dates that are both quality- and solution-robust. To this end, we compare several robustness measures and local search algorithms that use these measures. We start with an extensive simulation study where we determine the correlation of 13 existing and 6 new robustness measures with both quality and solution robustness. Next, we use the measures with high robustness correlation as the objective in our local search algorithm to find the best way to generate schedules containing both job-machine assignments as well as buffer assignments. We use a new dynamic objective weight within our local search algorithms, which actively changes the objective weights in each iteration. We found that the best way to generate robust schedules is to use robustness measures that model the processing times with normal distribution approximations and to combine job placement and buffer assignment simultaneously.
item.dc:creator: Casper Loman, Loriana Pascual, Bram Elderhorst, Marjan van den Akker, Roel van den Broek, Han Hoogeveen

item.title: Worst-Case and Covariance-Reconstruction Robust Adaptive Beamforming: Equivalence and Closed-Form Solution
item.description: arXiv:2603.09300v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robust adaptive beamforming (RAB) has developed along two separate lines. The worst-case-constrained approach guards against steering vector mismatch with a bounded uncertainty set, but suffers from desired signal cancellation at high input signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The covariance-reconstruction approach instead estimates the interference-plus-noise covariance matrix and solves for the mismatch numerically. We prove that the two are related by primal-dual equivalence: once the worst-case beamformer is normalized, it coincides exactly with the reconstruction-based one, so both reduce to one formulation. The signal cancellation of the worst-case approach is a consequence of its parameter choice, not of the formulation. For the unified problem we develop a closed-form solution in three stages: Diagonalization Transform, Phase Alignment, and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) Solution. Instead of solving for the Lagrange multiplier, we introduce an auxiliary variable that reduces the KKT system to a single scalar equation solvable by bisection. For an $N$-sensor array the cost is $\mathcal{O}(N^{3})$, the same order as the Lagrange-equation-based RMVB and well below the $\mathcal{O}(N^{3.5})$ of a second-order cone program, and it covers the rank-deficient case that RMVB excludes. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for existence and uniqueness, including a case where the feasible set is nonempty yet no optimal solution exists, and show that the Lagrange multiplier fixes the optimal value. Simulations confirm that, with matching parameters, the worst-case beamformer attains the output signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) of the reconstruction-based one, and that the closed-form solution reproduces the optimum of convex solvers in a fraction of their time.
item.dc:creator: Licheng Zhao, Rui Zhou, Wenqiang Pu, Daniel P. Palomar

item.title: A Level Set Method with Secant Iterations for the Least-Squares Constrained Nuclear Norm Minimization
item.description: arXiv:2603.12812v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an efficient algorithm for least-squares constrained nuclear norm minimization, a computationally challenging problem with broad applications. Our approach combines a level set method with secant iterations and a proximal generation method. As a key theoretical contribution, we establish the nonsingularity of the Clarke generalized Jacobian for a general class of projection norm functions over closed convex sets. This property and the (strong) semismoothness of our value function yield fast local convergence of the secant method. For the resulting nuclear norm regularized subproblems, we develop a proximal generation method that exploits low-rank structures without compromising convergence. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the superior performance of our approach compared to state-of-the-art methods.
item.dc:creator: Chiyu Ma, Jiaming Ma, Defeng Sun

item.title: Investigating mixed-integer programming approaches for the $p$-$\alpha$-closest-center problem
item.description: arXiv:2603.13214v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we introduce and study the $p$-$\alpha$-closest-center problem ($p\alpha$CCP), which generalizes the $p$-second-center problem, a recently emerged variant of the classical $p$-center problem. In the $p\alpha$CCP, we are given sets of customers and potential facility locations, distances between each customer and potential facility location as well as two integers $p$ and $\alpha$. The goal is to open facilities at $p$ of the potential facility locations, such that the maximum $\alpha$-distance between each customer and the open facilities is minimized. The $\alpha$-distance of a customer is defined as the sum of distances from the customer to its $\alpha$ closest open facilities. If $\alpha$ is one, the $p\alpha$CCP is the $p$-center problem, and for $\alpha$ being two, the $p$-second-center problem is obtained, for which the only existing algorithm in literature is a variable neighborhood search (VNS). We present four mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulations for the $p\alpha$CCP, strengthen them by adding valid and optimality-preserving inequalities and conduct a polyhedral study to prove relationships between their linear programming relaxations. Moreover, we present iterative procedures for lifting some valid inequalities to improve initial lower bounds on the optimal objective function value of the $p\alpha$CCP and characterize the best lower bounds obtainable by this iterative lifting approach. Based on our theoretical findings, we develop a branch-and-cut algorithm (B&C) to solve the $p\alpha$CCP exactly. We improve its performance by a starting and a primal heuristic, variable fixings and separating inequalities. In our computational study, we investigate the effect of the various ingredients of our B&C on benchmark instances from related literature. Our B&C is able to prove optimality for 17 of the 40 instances from the work on the VNS heuristic.
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth Gaar, Sara Joosten, Markus Sinnl

item.title: A Homotopy Framework for Constrained Multiobjective Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2605.00003v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a homotopy continuation framework for computing Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) points of constrained multiobjective optimization problems. The proposed homotopy map continuously deforms an easily solvable system into the KKT system associated with the original multiobjective problem, yielding a deterministic continuation path. Under the stated regularity and reference-point cone avoidance assumptions, we establish the existence of a smooth, bounded continuation path whose set of accumulation points as the homotopy parameter approaches zero is nonempty and consists of KKT points. The framework is implemented using two numerical continuation algorithms including an enhanced pseudo-arclength predictor--corrector strategy with adaptive step-size control and branch-restarting mechanisms to improve robustness for challenging nonconvex and degenerate problems. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method remains effective even when initialized from nonfeasible points, indicating practical robustness beyond the theoretical guarantees. Comparative studies evaluate the proposed framework against classical scalarization approaches and the evolutionary algorithms. Experiments on benchmark problems, disconnected and nonconvex multiobjective problems, analytically solvable three-objective problems, and a multiobjective IEEE 5-bus optimal power flow problem demonstrate the ability of the framework to compute KKT points in a variety of constrained settings. The results also highlight the effects of initialization and the limitations of continuation-based methods in recovering complete Pareto-front coverage. Overall, the proposed framework provides a deterministic and interpretable approach to computing Pareto-critical (KKT) points in constrained multiobjective optimization.
item.dc:creator: Olaoluwa Ogunleye, Guangming Yao, Jianhua Zhang, Manh Bui

item.title: Nonconvex Composite Functional Constraints via First-Order Augmented Lagrangian Methods under Local Regularity
item.description: arXiv:2607.08954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study nonasymptotic convergence of primal-dual methods for a class of nonconvex constrained optimization problems under local multiplier regularity. Both the objective and functional inequality constraints are compositions of convex Lipschitz outer functions with smooth nonlinear mappings. Unlike existing analyses requiring regularity globally or along the entire iterate sequence, we impose multiplier regularity only near the feasible set. Using an auxiliary minimax problem with a compact dual set, we derive Lyapunov estimates that identify nearly feasible iterates under feasible initialization and a sufficiently large penalty, without assuming multiplier boundedness. Local regularity then bounds the associated multipliers and makes dual truncation inactive, yielding approximate KKT certificates for the original problem. The smoothed prox-linear augmented Lagrangian method with dual regularization yields an $O(K^{-1/3})$ KKT residual rate. Without regularization, piecewise linear outer functions and additional local structural assumptions yield a local dual error bound and the sharper $O(K^{-1/2})$ rate.
item.dc:creator: Linglingzhi Zhu, Jiajin Li

item.title: Averaged proximal reflected gradient method for monotone variational inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2609.06409v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Projected reflected gradient (PRG) method proposed by Malitsky is efficient for solving monotone variational inequality (MVI), while the existing upper bound of step size is not tight due to the inequality scaling in the theoretical analysis. In this paper, we construct an averaged variant of PRG method for more general MVI and present a novel Lyapunov function to establish convergent theory. This averaged PRG method provides an improvement of the golden ratio algorithm [Y, Malitsky, Math. Program., 184, 383-410, 2020], and the involved step size is compatible with that for the classical methods, such as Popov's extragradient and forward-reflected-backward methods. Moreover, a fully adaptive strategy without linesearch is presented to adjust step sizes, which generates closed-form and potentially much larger step sizes. Numerical experiments on the Nash-Cournot equilibrium, HpHard, and image reconstruction problems demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: published in Computational Optimization and Applications, 2026
item.dc:creator: Xiaokai Chang, Jialin Li, Jun Yang

item.title: Minimax Oracle Call Complexity, Rounds and Admissible Noise in Zeroth-Order Optimization of Highly Smooth Functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.05517v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study zeroth-order optimization of convex and strongly convex functions with H\"older smoothness of order $\beta>2$ from values corrupted by random noise with bias independent of the method's random directions, a Lipschitz systematic error and a bounded adversarial error. We measure the number of function evaluations (calls), of sequential rounds of parallel calls, and the largest tolerable systematic and adversarial errors. For strongly convex functions with a bounded Hessian, we prove a lower bound of order $d^2\varepsilon^{-\beta/(\beta-1)}$ on the number of calls, where $d$ is the dimension and $\varepsilon$ the accuracy, and find the sharp power of $d$ under the stronger Hilbert--Schmidt smoothness for all $\beta>2$. An accelerated finite-difference method attains them in $O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ rounds for condition number $\kappa$, like Nesterov's method with exact gradients, and tolerates the optimal systematic and, up to logarithms, adversarial errors; rate-optimal methods need $\Omega(\log d)$ rounds. The same number of calls is attained when the Hessian grows at most linearly with the gradient and, for centered noise, without an upper bound on the Hessian, also in logarithmically many rounds. For convex functions, our lower bound improves the known one polynomially in $d$ and is tight at the curvature of the hard instances; the systematic level is again optimal. These bounds extend to general norms and constraints; on the $\ell_1$ ball, mirror descent needs calls nearly linear in $d$. Experiments confirm the theory.
item.dc:creator: Timofei Loginov, Darina Dvinskikh, Nazarii Tupitsa, Osman Osmanov, Yuriy Dorn, Alexander Gasnikov

item.title: Distributionally Robust Regularization of Sparse Integer Programming Trained Learning Models
item.description: arXiv:2311.01994v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Building explainable machine learning models is crucial for human users to be able to interpret the proposed statistical relationship obtained from the training data. Mixed-integer optimization formulations are often used to train such models with explicit sparsity constraints, aiming to strike the right trade-off between sparsity and prediction accuracy. Existing methods to find the right choice of sparsity -- e.g., via cross-validation -- are computationally expensive. For convex model training formulations, recent advances in distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provide strong generalization while sidestepping this computational burden. We describe an extension of such regularization via DRO to mixed-integer sparse programs, providing statistical guarantees as a function of an associated sparsity parameter of the formulation. We illustrate the use of this approach in the case of building explainable binary classification models using sets of feature value rules.
item.dc:creator: Sanjeeb Dash, Soumyadip Ghosh, Joao Goncalves, Mark S. Squillante

item.title: Adaptive Dead-Zone Dual Sliding Mode Observer for Reliable Electrochemical Model-Based SOC Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2508.21610v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate state-of-charge (SOC) estimation is essential for safe and efficient lithium-ion battery operation. Electrochemical models provide physically grounded SOC estimates, but nonlinear voltage dynamics and coupled state-parameter errors can destabilize online adaptation. This paper proposes an adaptive dead-zone dual sliding-mode observer (ADZ-DSMO) based on an improved extended single-particle (IESP) model. A state SMO estimates SOC-related states, while a parameter SMO updates dominant model parameters. An online-computable, Lyapunov-guided adaptive boundary selectively gates parameter updates while the state observer remains active at every sampling step. Validation on a Panasonic NCR18650PF cell under 1C and 3C constant-current discharge and the Urban Dynamometer Driving Schedule (UDDS) and New European Driving Cycle (NEDC) profiles shows lower SOC estimation errors than conventional dual SMO and the IESP-based dual extended Kalman filter (DEKF). Compared with DEKF, the proposed observer provides faster recovery from a 30% initial SOC bias. Selective parameter updating reduces the average per-step computation time compared with the always-updating dual SMO. Temperature tests and capacity-based, model-generated aging cases further assess robustness. These results support adaptive gating as a means of reducing error propagation and computational overhead in electrochemical-model-based joint state-parameter estimation.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Applied Energy, Volume 427, Part D, Article 129043 (2027)
item.dc:creator: Guangdi Hu, Keyi Liao, Jian Ye, Feng Guo

item.title: Arithmetic Circuits and Neural Networks for Regular Matroids
item.description: arXiv:2511.02406v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that there exist uniform $(+,\times,/)$-circuits of size $O(n^3)$ to compute the basis generating polynomial of regular matroids on $n$ elements. By tropicalization, this implies that there exist uniform $(\max,+,-)$-circuits and ReLU neural networks of the same size for weighted basis maximization of regular matroids. As a consequence in linear programming theory, we obtain a first example where taking the difference of two extended formulations can be more efficient than the best known individual extended formulation for the base polytope of regular matroids of size $O(n^6)$ by Aprile and Fiorini. Such differences have recently been introduced as virtual extended formulations. The proof of our main result relies on a fine-tuned version of Seymour's decomposition of regular matroids which allows us to identify and maintain graphic substructures to which we can apply a local version of the star-mesh transformation.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Hertrich, Stefan Kober, Georg Loho

item.title: Set Membership Estimation for Stochastic Linear Contextual Bandits
item.description: arXiv:2606.20022v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Contextual bandit learning has attracted increasing attention in engineering applications due to its ability to incorporate side/context information in time-varying environments. A widely used approach for contextual bandits is optimism in the face of uncertainty (OFU), in which uncertainty sets for unknown parameters are constructed and decisions are made optimistically over these sets. In the bandit literature, uncertainty sets are typically derived using statistical learning tools, such as confidence intervals. In contrast, set membership estimation (SME), a well-established uncertainty quantification approach in control and system identification, has received little attention in the bandit literature. This paper investigates the connection between SME and contextual bandits by focusing on linear contextual bandits as a starting point. We propose an SME-based OFU algorithm and establish a sublinear regret bound under proper assumptions. Simulations further demonstrate the promising performance of SME-OFU compared with existing methods. This supplementary manuscript provides more proof details in Section IV and the Appendix.
item.dc:creator: Haonan Xu, Yingying Li

item.title: The Normal Procrustes Problem: A Riemannian Optimization Approach
item.description: arXiv:2608.19513v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For given $m \times n$ data matrices $X, Y$, we investigate the Normal Procrustes Problem---the least squares optimization problem that aims to minimize $\|AX-Y\|_F^2$, where $A$ is constrained to be a normal $m \times m$ matrix. As far as the author of this article is aware, no other method that attempts to solve the Normal Procrustes Problem exists in the literature; we thus propose what is, to our knowledge, the first such method. We, furthermore, adapt our approach to address the Real Normal Procrustes Problem, where $A$ must be real. In our treatment of these problems, we first reduce our complex and real objective functions to be purely optimizable over the Riemannian manifolds of the unitary and real orthogonal matrices, respectively. This reduction enables us to apply techniques in Riemannian manifold optimization to approximate solutions to both. The Closest Normal Matrix and Real Closest Normal Matrix Problems are both special cases of their respective Procrustes Problems (by setting $m = n$ and $X = I_m$) and have been previously studied in the literature. Our approach thus recovers a novel Riemannian optimization method for approximating solutions to both these problems. We further numerically test the performance of our method across all such problems (including against previously developed algorithms on the Closest Normal Matrix Problems) and obtain competitive residuals and favorable scaling in wall-clock time.
item.dc:creator: Kyle Bierly

item.title: Global Multi-Maturity SPX-VIX Calibration Beyond Markovian Stitching
item.description: arXiv:2609.04087v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a global martingale optimal transport framework for joint S&P 500 (SPX)-VIX smile calibration across multiple maturities, without the conditional independence that Markovian stitching imposes between months. We prove that exact local and global feasibility are equivalent, yet the stitched laws, which carry earlier months only through the current SPX level, can form a strict subset of the global ones, so adjacent smiles cannot identify the dependence across months. We show that relative entropy against the standard Markov reference selects the stitched law, so this dependence must be supplied deliberately. We supply it through a finite-memory reference, in which a latent autoregressive state drives the VIX levels while every VIX marginal stays exact, and calibrate the resulting law on a junction tree whose size grows linearly with the number of maturities. On market data with up to nine SPX maturities, a law with memory and a law without it fit the same quotes but price VIX-conditioned SPX Asian claims differently: on every calendar, memory makes a claim on the maximum VIX cheaper and a claim on the minimum VIX dearer. Varying the memory strength on one calendar moves these differences steadily from zero, so the vanilla quotes, which fix the law of each date, do not determine prices that depend on the joint law across dates.
item.dc:creator: Atithi Acharya, Charlie Che, Yue Sun, Brandon Augustino, Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Shree Hari Sureshbabu

item.title: Minimizing the makespan in job shop scheduling under conflict graph constraints
item.description: arXiv:2609.04161v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the job shop scheduling problem with a conflict graph, in which adjacent jobs cannot be processed simultaneously on different machines, with the objective of minimizing the makespan. We establish a polynomial equivalence with a resource-constrained job shop problem having unit-capacity resources and binary resource requirements The problem is strongly NP-hard even on two machines with unit-time operations. For this setting, we derive an optimal-makespan formula and a linear-time algorithm when the conflict graph is a cluster graph, given the clique partition. We also develop a polynomial-time $4/3$-approximation algorithm for arbitrary conflict graphs on two machines when each job has exactly two unit-time operations. For the general problem, we propose four mixed-integer linear formulations, lower bounds, and a genetic algorithm with active, non-delay, and hybrid decoding procedures. Computational experiments on instances derived from the Lawrence and Taillard benchmarks and on randomly generated generalized job shop instances evaluate the proposed methods and show that the genetic algorithm generally improves on constructive heuristics.
item.dc:creator: Nour Elhouda Tellache, Abdenour Azerine

item.title: Unique Minimizers for Permanents, Mixed Discriminants, and Log-concave Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2609.21083v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The permanent and mixed discriminant of positive matrices are classic problems for which we do not expect an efficient algorithm for exact computation. Thus much work has been done to understand how well we can bound and approximately compute these quantities. One line of research in this area begins with the results of the first author, where van der Waerden lower bounds of $\frac{n!}{n^n}$ are proven for doubly stochastic inputs for both problems, using a simple proof via stable polynomials. Along with the bound itself, the same techniques are used to show that the permanent and mixed discriminant are uniquely minimized at a certain natural symmetric input. In this paper, we generalize those results in two ways. First, we extend the unique minimization results beyond doubly stochastic inputs to other marginals which are near doubly stochastic. This yields the first such unique minimization results for the mixed discriminant beyond the doubly stochastic case. We also discuss why one cannot hope similar results to hold in general for all marginals. Second, we extend the unique minimization result for real stable polynomials to strongly log-concave (aka Lorentzian) polynomials in the doubly stochastic case. This captures an analogous previous result on unique minimization for the mixed volume. Finally, we discuss various open problems related to these results.
item.dc:creator: Leonid Gurvits, Jonathan Leake

item.title: CNet: A Complex-Valued Deep Learning Framework with Wirtinger Autodifferentiation and FFT--Hadamard Convolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.08592v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: CNet is a C++/CUDA framework for deep complex-valued neural networks (CVNNs), trained by gradient descent with explicit Wirtinger (CR-calculus) derivatives. Complex models are underexplored yet natural where data is intrinsically complex -- RF/IQ, MRI k-space, radar/SAR, audio spectra -- and phase carries information real networks discard. CNet is physics-native: a network is a cascade of complex (often unitary) operations on an amplitude vector, and classification is a Born-rule measurement p_k = |z_k|^2 / ||z||^2 rather than a softmax over real logits. Every layer ships a CPU reference and a finite-difference-verified CUDA kernel; the static, batch-cloned computation graph captures cleanly into CUDA Graphs, outperforming eager and compiled torch.complex64 on an H100. We present three studies. (1) A fully complex causal language model, built on a new causal (triangular-masked) Fourier mixer with an O(N log N) Bluestein evaluation of the forward pass and its Wirtinger adjoint, matches a parameter-matched real causal FNet on character-level tiny-shakespeare in under half the steps. We introduce Born-rule attention, a content-based causal mixer whose weights are the quantum-measurement probabilities |<Q_k, K_j>|^2 -- to our knowledge the first classical, complex-valued attention to replace softmax with the squared-magnitude Born score; with rotary embeddings and per-token complex normalization it reaches 1.52 nats/char, matching softmax self-attention, and transfers unchanged to byte-level (1.31 nats/char) and sub-word WikiText-103. (2) On radio-modulation classification (RML2016.10a/RML22) we trace the pooled-power accuracy ceiling to discarded temporal structure and recover it with a learnable cyclostationary conjugate-lag operator. (3) A bottleneck analysis of the Fourier phase problem in coherent-diffraction imaging isolates where complex-valued networks still need new operators.
item.dc:creator: Marcel Crasmaru

item.title: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL
item.description: arXiv:2610.08989v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space. However, naively optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic. In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges. We introduce LASER, a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time. Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER. Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/.
item.dc:creator: Songyuan Zhang, Oswin So, Eric Yang Yu, Matthew Cleaveland, Peter Crowley-Dolen, Chuchu Fan

item.title: Identifiability of a dissipative knowledge-dynamics model: exact recovery under designed excitation, degeneration on observational data
item.description: arXiv:2610.09889v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human learning is a dissipative dynamical process: mastery accumulates through practice, decays through forgetting, and propagates across interdependent concepts. We model it as a nonlinear dissipative system of ordinary differential equations whose parameters are mechanistically meaningful (a transfer-of-practice matrix, per-concept forgetting rates, and a saturating practice-response gain), and we study when those parameters can actually be recovered from data. For two concepts, we prove a constructive structural identifiability theorem for the associated inverse problem under explicit excitation conditions, together with monotonicity, robustness and L-stability results. We derive an implicit L-stable scheme and a batched solver numerically equivalent to the per-trajectory formulation yet two orders of magnitude faster. The empirical study is two-sided. Under the theorem's excitation conditions, synthetic recovery is exact. On large observational benchmarks it is not. An apparently strong recovery, with forgetting rates correlating with topic error rates at Spearman $\rho = 0.83$, is refuted by four controls: it survives destroying the temporal order of the data, is matched by a classical Bayesian baseline, and is unaffected by removing real timestamps. A single shared forgetting rate attains the same accuracy, and replaying the real schedule with identical true rates reproduces most of the correlation. A positive control shows that the controls detect forgetting where it is observable. We trace the effect to the stationary structure of the model and show that it is consistent with the degeneration anticipated by the theory in the absence of designed excitation.
item.dc:creator: Arman Kostanian, Armen Beklaryan
